title: The stubborn past
title_target: Eu fui, eu fiz, eu tive
goal: Round off the past tense with the irregular verbs — ten words that show up in nearly every story, and whose forms must be learned whole.
bekal: telling a whole experience in a few sentences in a row
recognizing that *fui* has two meanings at once

notes: ⚠️ **Fui means both "I went" and "I was".** The verbs *ser* and *ir* share their entire past tense — *fui, foi, fomos, foram* — and have done since Latin times. Only context separates them: *Eu fui ao mercado* (I went to the market) versus *Eu fui professor* (I used to be a teacher). In practice this overlap hardly ever causes trouble, because direction is always marked by a preposition.

**Como foi…?** is the most useful question in this unit. *Como foi o seu dia?*, *Como foi a viagem?*, *Como foi a prova?* — one formula for asking how something went. The standard answers: *Foi ótimo*, *Foi tranquilo*, *Foi difícil*.

**Não quis means "I didn't want to", not "I couldn't".** *Querer* in the past has a firm tone: *ele não quis ajudar* means he **refused** to help, not just that he didn't get around to it. This small difference sometimes causes misunderstandings.

**Aí is the most typically Brazilian story connector.** Literally "there", but in a story it means "then", "so", "and then". Brazilians string whole stories together with *aí*: *Aí eu cheguei, aí ele falou, aí a gente saiu*. Just like "so then…" in an English anecdote.

**Todo mundo passa por isso** = "everyone goes through that". *Passar por* means "to go through, to experience", and it's one of the most comforting things to hear when you're struggling in a foreign country.

grammars.title: Ten irregular past-tense verbs
body: There's no pattern. Learn them the way you'd learn a list of phone numbers — and the consolation: after this table, there's almost nothing left to learn whole at A1 level.
after: **The second and third columns are the ones you'll use most**, because stories are usually about "I" or "he/she". If you're short on time, learn those two columns first and the rest will follow.
⚠️ Notice the last two rows: *dizer* and *querer* use the **same** form for *eu* and *ele* (*disse*, *quis*). Once again, one less thing to memorize.

**Tricky pronunciations:** *fiz* = FEES, *fez* = FAYS, *quis* = KEES, *disse* = JEE-see, *veio* = VEY-oo, *deu* = DAYW, *viu* = VEEW. Note that a final *-z* is pronounced **s**, as the pronunciation chapter explains.

grammars.title: Linking a story together
body: Linking words that turn a pile of sentences into a story.
after: A complete story: *Primeiro eu cheguei no aeroporto. Depois peguei um táxi. Aí o motorista falou comigo, mas eu não entendi nada. Então eu mostrei o endereço no celular. Por fim, cheguei em casa às onze da noite.*
The best practice for this unit: write five sentences about your first day somewhere new, using the first five linking words in order.

grammars.title: Já and ainda não
body: Two little words that attach to the past tense and settle the "already or not yet" question.
after: **Já + past tense also means "ever".** *Você já foi ao Brasil?* = "Have you ever been to Brazil?" Portuguese doesn't need a special form for experiences like English "have been"; the ordinary past tense is enough.
⚠️ Answering "not yet" with just *não* sounds curt and can be taken as a flat "no". Use **ainda não** — two words, and much friendlier.

sections.title: A short story: um dia ruim

blocks.text: Read it aloud. Every verb is in the past tense, and most of them are irregular.

head: Português
English
rows: *Eu acordei tarde porque o despertador não tocou.*
I woke up late because the alarm didn't go off.
I didn't have time for breakfast.
*Fui de metrô, mas o metrô quebrou.*
I took the subway, but the subway broke down.
*Aí eu peguei um ônibus e cheguei uma hora atrasado.*
So I caught a bus and arrived an hour late.
*O meu chefe não disse nada, mas ele viu.*
My boss didn't say anything, but he saw.
I wanted to explain, but I couldn't.
In the end, everything worked out.

blocks.text: **Dar certo** literally "to give right", means "to work out, to succeed". Its opposite is *dar errado* (to go wrong). Together with *dá para* from unit 12, the verb *dar* turns out to cover a huge number of everyday expressions.

**Conseguir** deserves attention: it means "to manage to do", and it's often used where English simply says "can" or "could". *Não consegui dormir* = "I couldn't sleep", *Consegui chegar a tempo* = "I managed to arrive on time".

items: I'll call you later → *Te ligo depois*
Help me, please → *Me ajuda, por favor*
Is this for me? → *É para mim?*
I don't know him → *Eu não conheço ele*
